problem: "closet" (period sense: small room) reads today as a wardrobe, so Jane seems to sleep in a cupboard; "crib" (period: small bed) reads as a baby's cot for a ten-year-old.
new_text: It was barely five o'clock on the morning of January nineteenth when Bessie brought a candle into my little bedroom and found me already up and nearly dressed. I had risen half an hour before she came in and had washed my face and put on my clothes by the light of a half-moon just setting, its rays streaming through the narrow window near my bed. I was to leave Gateshead that day on a coach that passed the lodge gates at six in the morning. Bessie was the only person up yet. She had lit a fire in the nursery and now set about making my breakfast. Few children can eat when excited about a journey, and I was no exception. After Bessie pressed me in vain to take a few spoonfuls of the boiled milk and bread she'd prepared, she wrapped some biscuits in paper and put them in my bag. Then she helped me into my coat and bonnet, wrapped herself in a shawl, and together we left the nursery. As we passed Mrs. Reed's bedroom, she asked, "Will you go in and say good-bye to the Missus?"

problem: "crib" reads as a baby's cot to a modern reader; use "bed" (consistent with the 5.0 fix).
new_text: "No, Bessie. She came to my bedside last night when you were down at supper and said I needn't disturb her in the morning, or my cousins either. She told me to remember that she had always been my best friend and to speak well of her and be grateful to her."

problem: "tall, fair" will be read as blonde, which clashes with her very dark brown hair in the same paragraph (and dark hair in 5.23). The intended sense is fair-skinned.
new_text: While this was carried out, the lady moved slowly up the room. I must have a strong instinct for reverence, because I still remember the admiring awe with which I watched her. Seen now in full daylight, she was tall, fair-skinned, and well-proportioned. Brown eyes with a kindly light and a fine fringe of long lashes softened the whiteness of her broad forehead. Her hair, very dark brown, was arranged in round curls at each temple, in the fashion of the time, when neither smooth bands nor long ringlets were in style. Her dress, also fashionable, was purple cloth trimmed with a sort of Spanish pattern in black velvet. A gold watch (watches were less common then) shone at her waist. Add to this picture refined features, a complexion pale but clear, and a stately bearing, and you will have, at least as clearly as words can give it, a correct idea of the appearance of Miss Temple—Maria Temple, as I later saw the name written in a prayer book I was given to carry to church.

problem: The Eutychus allusion and the "third loft" joke are unintelligible without knowing the story (Acts 20: a young man fell asleep during St. Paul's sermon and fell from a third-floor window). A brief in-line gloss makes the joke land.
new_text: Sunday evenings were spent reciting the Church Catechism and chapters five, six, and seven of St. Matthew by heart, and listening to a long sermon read by Miss Miller, whose irrepressible yawns showed how tired she was. A frequent interruption was half a dozen little girls playing the part of Eutychus, the young man in Acts who dozed off during St. Paul's sermon and fell from a third-story window: overwhelmed by sleep, they would fall down—if not out of the third loft, then off the fourth bench—and be picked up half dead. The remedy was to push them into the center of the schoolroom and make them stand until the sermon was done. Sometimes their legs gave out and they collapsed in a heap. Then they were propped up with the monitors' tall stools.

problem: "left alone by everyone else" reads as being ignored or shunned, contradicting "welcomed"; the sense is that no one bullied or bothered her.
new_text: Before the half hour was up, five o'clock struck. School was dismissed and everyone went to the dining hall for tea. I dared to climb down from the stool. It was deep dusk. I retreated to a corner and sat on the floor. The spell that had sustained me began to dissolve. Reaction set in, and soon the grief that seized me was so overwhelming that I collapsed face-down on the floor. Now I cried. Helen Burns wasn't there. Nothing held me up. Left to myself, I gave in completely, and my tears soaked the floorboards. I had meant to be so good, and to do so much at Lowood—to make friends, earn respect, and win affection. That very morning I had already made real progress: I'd reached the head of my class. Miss Miller had praised me warmly. Miss Temple had smiled with approval and promised to teach me drawing and let me start French if I kept improving for another two months. I had been welcomed by my fellow students—treated as an equal by those my age, and not bothered by anyone else. And now here I was, crushed and trampled again. Would I ever be able to rise?

problem: The rhetorical question is followed by "That was the nature of Helen's speech", which does not answer or connect to it and reads as a non-sequitur on first listening.
new_text: The good food, the warm fire, the presence and kindness of her beloved teacher, or perhaps more than all of these, something in her own extraordinary mind, had awakened her powers. They stirred, they caught fire: first glowing in the bright flush of her cheek, which until this hour I had only ever seen pale and bloodless; then shining in the liquid brilliance of her eyes, which had suddenly acquired a beauty more striking than Miss Temple's—a beauty not of fine color or long lashes or sculpted brows, but of meaning, of animation, of radiance. Then her soul sat on her lips, and words flowed from a source I cannot name. Does a fourteen-year-old girl have a heart large enough, strong enough, to hold the swelling spring of pure, passionate eloquence? Yet such eloquence was exactly what marked Helen's speech on that memorable evening. Her spirit seemed to be racing to live as much in a brief span as many live in a long lifetime.

problem: "etre" is missing its accent (être), and listeners with no French won't know it is the verb "to be".
new_text: Freed from that crushing weight, I set to work again from that hour, determined to push through every difficulty. I worked hard, and my success matched my effort. My memory, not naturally strong, improved with practice. Exercise sharpened my mind. Within a few weeks I was promoted to a higher class. In less than two months I was allowed to start French and drawing. I learned the first two tenses of the verb être (to be) and sketched my first cottage (whose walls, I should mention, rivaled the leaning tower of Pisa in their slope) on the same day. That night, going to bed, I forgot to fantasize about the imaginary feast of hot roast potatoes or fresh bread and milk that I usually conjured to comfort my hunger. Instead I feasted on visions of ideal drawings, all created by my own hands—freely sketched houses and trees, picturesque rocks and ruins, groups of cattle like those in a Cuyp painting, lovely paintings of butterflies hovering over rosebuds, birds picking ripe cherries, wren's nests holding pearl-like eggs wreathed in young ivy. I also pondered whether I would ever be able to translate fluently a certain little French story that Madame Pierrot had shown me that day. That problem was not solved to my satisfaction before I fell sweetly asleep.
